source.title: The Cost of Down-Scaling Language Models: Fact Recall Deteriorates before In-Context Learning
source.authors: Tian Jin; Nolan Clement; Xin Dong; Vaishnavh Nagarajan; Michael Carbin; Jonathan Ragan-Kelley; G. Dziugaite

page_placements.theme: Pruning and recovery have task- and budget-dependent response laws

record.tranche_reason: The study varies model size by pruning and by evaluating independently trained dense models, and measures task accuracy across sizes. It uses different outcomes from the original scaling-law studies and does not fit the claimed loss laws.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses scaling laws and reports pruning perplexity on C4 validation data (Appendix B, Table 2 and Figure 6), but does not fit power laws or test loss extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, or loss-based downstream prediction. The rows below cover reported downstream task accuracy across scale. Dense-scaling results are often summarized in text; exact curve values appear only in figures.
record.test_reason: Only the dense-scaling comparison bears on a version. It evaluates independently trained OPT models of different sizes, all with the same pretraining tokens, on curated QA and in-context-learning tasks (Section 6, Figure 4). That bears on V6, whether downstream accuracy improves with scale, in a task-specific setting. The study fits no curve, so predictability itself is untested. The pruning experiments remove weights from already-trained models. They measure compression robustness, not the scaling of trained models, so they fit no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that reducing model size, by pruning or by using a smaller dense model, harms fact recall beyond about 30% reduction but largely preserves in-context information processing up to 60–70% reduction. They frame this as a general property of scaling, and note in Appendix A that results may not generalise to all tasks and models.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates pruning and separately trained dense model sizes using task accuracy, rather than fitting held-out cross-entropy scaling laws or testing compute-optimal training allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by task type, pruning algorithm (SparseGPT versus Wanda), model family (including Pythia), and input dimension for linear ICL tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: One-shot pruning (SparseGPT, Wanda) of OPT, LLaMA and Pythia models degrades closed-book fact-recall accuracy at 20–40% sparsity. In-context tasks tolerate 50–70% sparsity within a 5% relative drop.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Post-training weight removal harms parametric fact recall before in-context learning ability.

fits_no_version.finding: C4 perplexity of pruned models rises slowly to about 50% sparsity, then sharply (e.g. LLaMA-13B: 6.6 dense, 59.9 at 80%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Perplexity degradation under one-shot pruning is nonlinear in sparsity.

record.problems: The main results concern a limited set of models and curated tasks. Many per-model curves are shown only in figures, and the paper reports threshold summaries rather than fitted predictive relationships. The authors state that results may not generalize across the full range of tasks and LLMs.
record.rows_left_out: No additional task-accuracy results were omitted. Perplexity results in Appendix B were not included because they do not test a fitted power law or another listed version; they report perplexity under pruning only.

untested.parts: No power-law fit of held-out loss. Table 2 perplexity is for pruned models, not trained models of different sizes.
No fixed-parameter shape comparison. Section 7 prunes attention versus FFW layers, which is not a shape sweep at fixed parameter count.
No other modality or training regime.
Predictability is untested: no fitted curve or loss-to-accuracy mapping. Dense scaling covers only the OPT family up to 30B.
No comparison of fits or exponents.

missing.what: Per-size OPT dense accuracies on each task, including which OPT sizes were evaluated. These exist only in Figure 4 and are needed to judge how accuracy scales with parameter count.
Separate dense-scaling rows for overriding QA (DisentQA) and each ICL task (linear, 2-layer NN, decision tree). Currently they are collapsed into r13.

record.verdict_notes: Training-token counts for OPT are inconsistent in the text. Section 3 says 180B tokens; Section 6 says all OPT models were trained on 300B tokens. The V6 evidence is thin: one model family, threshold summaries in the text, no fitted relationship. The pruning rows were reassigned to none because weight removal from a trained model is not the scaling the versions describe.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law fit for held-out loss against parameters, tokens, or compute; no test over several orders of magnitude with the other scaling variables controlled.
No small-run fit or forecast of larger-run loss.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or fitted parameter/token trends.
No comparison of architectures at fixed parameter count.
No other modality or training-regime scaling-law test.
The study measures task accuracy under down-scaling; it does not test forecasts based on pretraining loss, fit a predictive scaling curve, or evaluate a broad range of downstream benchmarks.
No comparison of loss-law exponents, compute-optimal splits, parameter-counting conventions, or fitting choices.

relationships.condition: OPT dense models, closed-book fact-recall QA (TriviaQA, WebQuestions)
relationships.reason: Accuracy rises with model size: dropping from 30B to 13B costs more than 5% relative accuracy (r9, r10). Predictability is not fitted.
relationships.display_finding: Reducing size from 30B to 13B decreased relative accuracy by more than 5%, without a fitted predictive relationship.

source_check.reason: Rows r9 and r10 show more than 5% relative accuracy loss from 30B to 13B, supporting improvement with scale in these tasks. Predictive fitting remains untested.

relationships.condition: OPT dense models, open-book QA, overriding QA and parameterised in-context learning tasks
relationships.reason: Accuracy barely improves with size: 6.7B is within 5% of 30B on open-book QA (r11, r12), and ICL is described as robust to down-scaling (r13). So gains from scale are task-dependent.
relationships.display_finding: The 6.7B model performed within 5% of 30B on open-book QA, and in-context learning remained robust to reductions in model size.

labels.label: limits_scope
labels.condition: OPT dense models, open-book QA, overriding QA and parameterised in-context learning tasks
labels.reason: Rows r11 and r12 retain accuracy within 5% when replacing 30B with 6.7B; Section 6 also explicitly describes overriding QA as less sensitive and parameterized ICL as robust to dense scaling. These results qualify the strength of downstream gains by task.

relation.reason: Section 6 reports the study's own downstream-accuracy comparisons across independently trained dense OPT sizes, bearing on V6.

tranche.reason: The dense-scaling results specifically qualify V6 through task dependence: fact recall benefits substantially from size, whereas contextual QA and parameterized ICL are much less sensitive. The introduction explicitly disputes similarly strong scaling gains for ICL.

source_check.notes: No predictive scaling curve or extrapolation is tested. The source inconsistently reports OPT training tokens as 180B in Section 3 and 300B in Section 6; Figure 8 also labels the larger LLaMA model 30B although the main setup specifies 33B.

statements.correction: Maximum sparsities within a 5% relative accuracy drop: SparseGPT, four-model mean—closed-book TriviaQA 30%, WebQuestions 40%; open-book TriviaQA(F) 50%, NaturalQuestions 60%; overriding DisentQA 70%; linear classification 60%, two-layer neural-network classification 60%, decision-tree classification 70%. SparseGPT, Pythia variants—closed-book TriviaQA 20%, open-book TriviaQA(F) 30%, linear classification 50%. Wanda—closed-book TriviaQA 30%, open-book TriviaQA 40%, linear classification 50%.
statements.problem: The 20–40% values are maximum sparsities retaining accuracy within the accepted drop, rather than levels already exceeding it. The 50–70% range fits parameterized ICL tasks but omits lower open-book thresholds among the cited rows.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Down-scaling on the tested QA and in-context learning tasks
reader_labels.reason: Accuracy sensitivity varies substantially by task: fact recall degrades at lower pruning levels than context-based QA and ICL, while dense down-scaling also has task-dependent effects; the paper does not test predictive fits. Rows r1-r13.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The reported tolerable sparsity thresholds differ across tasks and from the main SparseGPT results, qualifying how far the task-accuracy patterns generalize across model families and pruning methods. Rows r14-r19.
